title: Mars and Jupiter Are About to Meet in the Night Sky
summary:
Look up on the night of November 15-16, and you will see two planets putting on a show. Mars and Jupiter will appear just over one degree apart in the constellation Leo, closer than they have been in years. They will not be this close again until July 2029.

The pair will rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the United States. Below them, the blue-white star Regulus will glow. Mars will shine red, and Jupiter will shine bright beside it.

It is all a trick of perspective. In reality, Mars and Jupiter are separated by more than 368 million miles. The light from Regulus has traveled about 79 light-years to reach Earth. The planets only look close because they line up from our viewpoint.

Astronomers call this kind of meeting an appulse. It happens about once every two to two and a half years, when Mars catches up to Jupiter as the two planets travel around the sun. Jupiter is farther out, so Mars, moving on its closer, faster path, laps it from time to time.

Both Mars and Jupiter are what astronomers call superior planets, meaning their orbits lie beyond Earth's. Through a telescope, their disks always look full. Mercury and Venus, which orbit closer to the sun than Earth, show moon-like phases instead.

A six-inch telescope can show how different the two worlds are. Jupiter's giant bands of cloud ring the gas giant, made of ammonia and water moving in different directions through its hydrogen and helium air, pushed by powerful jet streams. Mars looks like a reddish, ochre disk with dark patches, where basalt rock has been swept clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface.
why_it_matters: Watching planets meet in the sky is a chance to see how the solar system moves, and it can turn anyone into a skywatcher for a night. Events like this happen only every few years, so they are worth stepping outside for.
